prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
When you type an HTTPS address into a browser and press Enter, the first thing the browser does is work out what you actually asked for. It parses the address into a scheme, a host name, an optional port, a path, and a query string, and it checks whether the host is on its HSTS list or has a preloaded rule, which would force the connection to use HTTPS even if you had typed plain HTTP. Before it touches the network, the browser also looks in its own caches. If it holds a fresh copy of the resource, according to the cache headers from an earlier visit, it can answer immediately and no network traffic is needed at all. A service worker registered for the site may also intercept the request at this point and decide what to return.

If the browser has to go to the network, it must first turn the host name into an IP address, because the internet routes packets by number rather than by name. It checks its own DNS cache, then asks the operating system, which checks its own cache and the local hosts file. If neither knows the answer, the request goes to a recursive resolver, usually run by your internet provider or a public service. That resolver may already have the answer cached. If it does not, it works down the hierarchy by asking a root server where to find the servers for the top-level domain, then asking those where to find the authoritative servers for the domain, and finally asking the authoritative server for the record itself. The answer comes back with a time-to-live that tells every cache along the way how long it may be reused. Modern browsers can also use encrypted DNS and may ask for IPv6 and IPv4 addresses together, preferring whichever connects first.

With an address in hand, the browser opens a connection. Classic HTTPS runs over TCP, which begins with a three-step handshake. The browser sends a SYN packet, the server replies with a SYN-ACK, and the browser acknowledges. This costs one full round trip before any useful data can flow, so the distance between you and the server matters a great deal. Newer versions of the protocol, HTTP/3, run over QUIC, which uses UDP and folds the transport setup and the encryption setup into a single exchange. A browser may learn that a site supports HTTP/3 from an earlier response header or from a DNS record, and it will often race the two approaches against each other.

Next comes the TLS handshake, which is what makes the connection secure rather than merely open. In the browser's first message, called the ClientHello, it names the host it wants through the Server Name Indication extension, lists the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, and includes its half of a key exchange. In TLS 1.3 this means the client guesses which key-exchange group the server will pick and sends a public value for it immediately, which saves a round trip compared with older versions. The server answers with its own key share, which lets both sides compute the same shared secret without ever sending it across the wire. Everything the server says after that point is encrypted. It sends its certificate chain, proof that it holds the private key matching that certificate, and a final message confirming that the handshake has not been tampered with.

The browser then decides whether to trust what it has been shown. It checks that the certificate covers the host name you asked for, that it falls within its validity dates, and that it chains up through intermediate certificates to a root authority the operating system or browser already trusts. It may also check revocation status, often through a stapled response that the server attached so the browser does not need to contact the authority itself. If any of these checks fail, you see the full-page warning rather than the site. If you have visited before, session resumption or a pre-shared key can let the browser skip much of this work, and TLS 1.3 even permits sending the first request alongside the handshake in some cases, though with some replay caveats.

Once both sides have the keys, the browser finally sends the HTTP request itself. The browser also decides which cookies belong to this request and attaches them. Over HTTP/1.1 the request is a block of readable text with a method such as GET, a path, a Host header, and headers describing the cookies, the languages and encodings the browser accepts, and so on. Over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 the same information travels as compressed binary frames, and many requests can share one connection at the same time. Whichever version is used, all of this is encrypted by TLS before it leaves your machine, so anyone watching the network can see roughly where the traffic is going but not what it says.

The request may not reach the server that built your page. It often lands first on a CDN edge node or a load balancer, which terminates the TLS connection, may answer from its own cache, and otherwise forwards the request to an origin server. The origin might run application code, query a database, or render a template, and all of that work happens before any reply is ready. That processing time is what developers measure as server think time.

The moment the first byte of the response comes back, the status line and headers beginning to arrive, is what performance tools call time to first byte. It is the sum of everything described above: redirects, DNS, the transport handshake, the TLS handshake, the request's travel, and the server's own work. Understanding where that time goes is the first step towards reducing it.
